title: How Narada caught devotion
hookLine: a maid's son sweeps the floor while holy men sing of God, and devotion takes root
carry: satsang: devotion is caught in holy company

cards: Long ago, in a house where holy men stayed through the rainy season, there was a small boy, the son of a maid. He swept, he fetched water, he sat quietly at the edge of the room while they sang and talked about God.
Sometimes, with their permission, he ate what was left on their plates. He was only a child. But something was happening to him.
The Bhagavata Purana says that boy became, in another life, Narada, the wandering sage with the veena who sings God's names through the worlds. Today, how devotion is caught.

teach.b: Narada tells this story himself, to the sage Vyasa. He says it was hearing those holy men, day after day, that woke love for God in him. Soon after, his mother died, and he set out alone.
In a forest, he sat under a tree, remembered what he'd heard, and the Lord appeared in his heart for a moment, then was gone. A voice told him the longing would stay, and it did, into his next life.
This is the teaching called satsang. Sat is the true, the real, the good.
Sang is company. Satsang is the company of the true: holy people, God, good words.
Many teachers put it simply: devotion is caught more than it's taught. You sit near people who love God, and love for God starts in you.
That's why Hindu families gather in living rooms to sing bhajans and call it a satsang. In the Swaminarayan tradition the word goes further. A devotee is a satsangi.
The weekly gathering is a satsang sabha. The whole fellowship, in Gujarat and far from it, is spoken of as the satsang.
In the Vachanamrut, Swaminarayan speaks of keeping company with God and with a true sadhu, a holy person who lives the teaching. So satsang isn't only a community's name. It's the method.
You come, you sit, you serve, you listen, even when you follow only part of it. A small boy at the edge of the room was enough to begin.

how: Swaminarayan devotees gather in weekly satsang assemblies at mandirs and in homes, with singing, readings from the scriptures and talks by sadhus or senior devotees.

o: a vow of silence kept by sadhus during retreats
satsang: the company of the true, where devotion is caught
a temple fee that makes someone a formal member

p: caught devotion serving holy men as a boy

s: in the Bhagavata, Narada was a great sage from the start
in an earlier life he was a maid's son who served visiting holy men and listened.
satsang is a word only the Swaminarayan tradition uses
it's an old word used across Hindu traditions; here it names the whole community.
in this tradition, satsang includes time near a true sadhu
being near a holy person who lives the teaching is itself a practice.

games.q: you're the boy Narada. the holy men are talking about God, and you're just a kid with a broom. what do you do?
o: leave; it isn't meant for someone like you.
keep serving and listening at the edge of the room.
pretend to understand so they'll let you stay.
games.why: he served and listened, and the Bhagavata says love for God woke in him from that company. that's satsang.

practice: Bring back a room where people were singing to God or speaking of something good, a temple, a living room, a school assembly, and sit at its edge in your mind, the way the boy did.

Let one line of a song, or one voice from that room, come back to you, and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, let it be a bhajan you know; if you don't, the voice of someone whose goodness rubbed off on you.

wordCard.voice: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, satsang, the company of the true, which woke devotion in Narada and names the whole Swaminarayan fellowship. Today's word.

orig.note: sat, the true or good, and sanga, company.

carryVoice: Your line: satsang, devotion is caught in holy company. A maid's son swept the floor and listened. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.5-1.6: Narada tells Vyasa of his earlier life as a maidservant's son who served visiting sages in the rainy season, heard them, and gained devotion
